title: With Due Respect (Vol. 5) -- Ch. 1: Subverting the Popular Will
keywords: Parish Pastoral Council for Responsible Voting
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5) -- CJP's April 1, 2007 Inquirer column, a civic-education primer exposing 'some of the ways used by politicians to subvert the popular will' across every stage of the electoral process, opening with the PPCRV's 'three Gs' (guns, goons, and gold) and the quipped fourth, 'Garci'

Cheating before and during election day -- padding voters' lists, 'flying' voters, fake or excess ballots and returns, 'nuisance' like-named candidates, the 'lansadera' ballot-swap scheme, vote-buying enforced by indelible ink, and intimidation with covert ballot-marking

Cheating after the ballots are cast -- misreading ballots at the precinct, and 'wholesale' fraud via 'dagdag-bawas' alteration of election returns and statements of votes (SOVs), with the decisive battles fought in 'pre-proclamation controversies' over the validity of the returns

Cheating after proclamation -- election protests before the proper tribunals, ballot substitution in the treasurers' custody, and 'dubious' rulings invalidating ballots as 'marked' or 'spoiled' without reason -- ending that 'eternal vigilance at all stages of the polls is the price of democracy'
sub_topics: The civic purpose: with candidate filing over, the 'vital public concern' is that 'every ballot is counted honestly, accurately, and speedily,' so CJP catalogues the cheats -- coded by the PPCRV as the 'three Gs' (guns, goons, gold), to which someone added 'Garci'

Pre-election cheats: padding the voters' list, registering 'flying' or unqualified voters, printing fake or excess ballots and returns, and -- 'more damaging' -- fielding 'like-named or nuisance candidates to invalidate ballots cast for the genuine aspirants'

The 'lansadera': a genuine ballot is 'spirited out of the polling place,' often with the connivance of the Board of Election Inspectors, filled in a safe house, and cast by a registered voter who returns the blank ballot he was given, the cycle repeating

Suppressing the opposing vote: paying hostile voters not to vote and marking a fingernail with indelible ink so they are barred, plus outright 'intimidation, bribery, terrorism or coercion,' with bought ballots covertly identified by quirks like middle names or peculiar name arrangements
Precinct-level fraud: 'misreading' the ballots -- names written are not read, names not written are 'read' -- so votes are illegally 'added to or subtracted from the tally'

'Wholesale' fraud ('dagdag-bawas'): altering or substituting the election returns and statements of votes (SOVs), where 'a change of one number, say, from 10 to 100' or an SOV 'from 1,000 to 10,000' can decide an election, since the SOVs feed the Boards of Canvassers' Certificates of Canvass and the proclamation

Pre-proclamation controversies: the 'critical struggles' after precinct counting but before proclamation turn on the validity of the election returns, demanding vigilance from lawyers and watchers -- yet many candidates 'spend all their resources during the... campaign, forgetting that the canvass requires even more vigilance'

After proclamation: results may be contested by 'timely election protests' (in the RTCs for municipal, the Comelec for provincial/city, and the House/Senate Electoral Tribunals for Congress), while cheats substitute ballots in the treasurers' custody -- and CJP cites Romulo Macalintal's example of a governor's race (margin 2,700) where the Comelec voided 3,500 of the winner's ballots as 'marked' though the ballot boxes' seals 'were still intact,' so 'until cheating is successfully checked by a credible Comelec... the popular will [is] subverted' and 'eternal vigilance at all stages of the polls is the price of democracy'
signature_phrases: eternal vigilance at all stages of the polls is the price of democracy

stances.claim: Politicians subvert the popular will at every stage -- before, during and after the vote -- through schemes from padding lists and 'lansadera' ballot-swaps to 'dagdag-bawas' alteration of returns and post-proclamation ballot substitution, so citizens must be vigilant throughout.
stances.rhetorical_move: systematic catalogue: walking the reader stage-by-stage through the fraud playbook to arm them against it

stances.claim: The decisive fight is often the canvass and the 'pre-proclamation controversies,' not the campaign -- yet candidates 'spend all their resources' campaigning and neglect the vigilance the canvass demands.
stances.rhetorical_move: misplaced-priorities warning: redirecting attention to where elections are actually won or stolen

stances.claim: 'Dubious' Comelec and trial-court rulings that void ballots as 'marked' or 'spoiled' without legal reason -- as in a governor's race where 3,500 ballots were invalidated though the boxes' seals were intact -- endanger democracy until a 'credible Comelec' checks the cheating.
stances.rhetorical_move: evidence-of-failure: using a concrete anomaly to indict adjudication, not just field-level fraud

notable_anecdotes: The fourth 'G': CJP notes the PPCRV's 'guns, goons, and gold' shorthand and the wry addition of a fourth -- 'Garci' -- invoking the wiretap scandal.
The 'lansadera' relay: he explains the ballot-swap scheme in which a filled-in ballot is smuggled in and cast while the blank one is carried back out, 'repeated on and on.'
Inked to silence: he describes paying hostile voters not to vote, then marking a fingernail with indelible ink so the law bars them from voting.

Sealed boxes, voided ballots: he relays Macalintal's example of a governor's race where the Comelec invalidated 3,500 ballots as 'marked' even though the ballot boxes had never been opened -- 'How then were the ballots examined?'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's April 1, 2007 Inquirer column, is a civic-education primer exposing 'the ways used by politicians to subvert the popular will' at every stage of an election. He opens with the PPCRV's 'three Gs' -- guns, goons, and gold -- and the quipped fourth, 'Garci.' Before and during election day, cheats pad the voters' list, register 'flying' voters, print fake or excess ballots and returns, and field 'nuisance' like-named candidates to spoil votes for genuine aspirants; the 'lansadera' scheme smuggles a pre-filled ballot into the box (often with BEI connivance) while the blank one is carried back out to be filled again; hostile voters are paid off and their fingernails inked so the law bars them; and bought ballots are covertly identified by quirks like middle names. After the ballots are cast, precinct 'misreading' adds or subtracts votes, while 'wholesale' fraud -- 'dagdag-bawas' -- alters the election returns and statements of votes (SOVs), where changing 'one number, say, from 10 to 100,' or an SOV 'from 1,000 to 10,000,' can decide a race, since the SOVs feed the Boards of Canvassers' Certificates of Canvass and the proclamation. The 'critical struggles,' he stresses, come after precinct counting but before proclamation, in 'pre-proclamation controversies' over the returns' validity -- a vigilance many candidates neglect after spending everything on the campaign. After proclamation, results may be contested by 'timely election protests' (RTCs for municipal offices, the Comelec for provincial/city, the House and Senate Electoral Tribunals for Congress), even as ballots are substituted in the treasurers' custody. He closes with a 'dubious' adjudication: a governor's race (margin 2,700) where the Comelec voided 3,500 of the winner's ballots as 'marked' even though the ballot boxes' seals were intact -- 'How then were the ballots examined?' -- concluding that until a 'credible Comelec' checks the cheating, 'eternal vigilance at all stages of the polls is the price of democracy.'
